title: Decomposition and abstraction
explanation: Decomposition breaks a large problem into smaller, manageable sub-problems. Abstraction removes unnecessary detail so you can focus on what matters for solving the problem, e.g. a bus map shows routes but not exact road shapes.

title: Flowcharts and pseudocode
explanation: Flowcharts represent an algorithm visually using standard shapes for start/end, process steps, and decisions. Pseudocode expresses the same logic in structured, plain-English-like statements, independent of any real language.

title: Searching and sorting algorithms
explanation: Linear search checks items one by one — works unsorted but slow. Binary search halves a sorted list each step — much faster. Bubble sort repeatedly swaps adjacent out-of-order items to sort a list, at the cost of being slow on large lists.

title: Sequence, selection and iteration
explanation: Every program combines three constructs: sequence (steps run in order), selection (if/elif/else to branch), and iteration (for/while to repeat).

title: Variables, constants and data types
explanation: A variable's value can change while a program runs; a constant is fixed. Core data types: integer, real/float, Boolean, character, and string.
code:
PI = 3.14159          # constant (by convention, not enforced)
radius = 4             # variable
area = PI * radius ** 2
print(area)

title: Arrays (1D and 2D)
explanation: A 1D array (Python list) stores an ordered sequence of values accessed by a single index. A 2D array stores values in a grid, accessed with a row and column index — useful for tables or game boards.

title: String handling
explanation: Strings can be sliced, searched, and transformed using built-in operations: getting length, changing case, extracting substrings, and joining/splitting.

title: Subprograms: functions and procedures
explanation: Breaking a program into subprograms makes it easier to read, test, and reuse. A function returns a value to the caller; a procedure carries out actions without necessarily returning one.

title: Input validation and testing
explanation: Validation rejects clearly wrong input before it's used (e.g. checking a mark is between 0 and 100). Testing a program should use normal, boundary, and erroneous data to confirm it behaves correctly in every case.

title: Binary and hexadecimal representation
explanation: Computers store everything as binary (0s and 1s). Hexadecimal is a compact way for humans to read binary, since each hex digit represents exactly 4 bits.

title: Units of data storage
explanation: Data is measured in bits and bytes (8 bits), scaling up through kilobytes, megabytes, gigabytes and terabytes, each roughly 1000 times the size of the previous unit.

title: Character sets and image representation
explanation: Character sets like ASCII and Unicode assign a unique number to every character a computer can display. A bitmap image is stored as a grid of pixels, where each pixel's colour is a binary value; more bits per pixel allows more colours.

title: Data compression
explanation: Compression makes files smaller. Lossless compression removes redundancy so the file can be perfectly restored; lossy compression permanently discards some detail for greater size savings (common for images/audio/video).

title: Hardware and the CPU
explanation: The CPU carries out the fetch-decode-execute cycle continuously: fetching the next instruction from memory, decoding what it means, then executing it. Its speed and number of cores affect overall performance.

title: Software: system vs application
explanation: System software (like the operating system) manages the computer itself — memory, processes, peripherals. Application software (like a word processor or web browser) lets the user perform specific tasks.

title: Network types and topologies
explanation: A LAN covers a small local area (e.g. one school); a WAN spans a wider area, often using third-party infrastructure like the internet. A star topology links every device to a central switch; failure of one cable doesn't take down the whole network.

title: The internet and protocols
explanation: The internet is a global network of networks. Protocols like TCP/IP govern how data is broken into packets and routed; HTTP/HTTPS govern how web pages are requested and delivered, with HTTPS adding encryption.

title: Network security threats
explanation: Common threats include malware, phishing (tricking users into revealing information), brute-force password attacks, and SQL injection, where malicious input is crafted to manipulate a database query.
code:
-- Never build a query by concatenating raw user input:
-- "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '" + input + "'"
-- Use a parameterised query instead, so input can't change the query's structure
SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = ?;

title: Legal, moral, ethical and environmental impacts
explanation: Computing raises real issues: data privacy and consent, laws such as the Computer Misuse Act (unauthorised access/modification) and the Data Protection Act/UK GDPR (how personal data must be handled), and the environmental cost of manufacturing devices and disposing of e-waste.
